newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU and U.S. in last ditch trade talks over Cuba.
newsitem.headline: EU and U.S. in last ditch trade talks over Cuba.

text.p: European and U.S. trade negotiators are expected to be in contact throughout the weekend in an attempt to resolve a punishing trade row over Cuba that comes to a head in Geneva on Monday.
"I can confirm that contacts are going on and will continue," said Peter Guilford, spokesman for European Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan.

The European Union is due to formally present its complaint against Washington's Helms-Burton Act at the World Trade Organisation (WTO) on Monday, the culmination of nearly a year of bitter wrangling.

The act -- an amalgamation of years of U.S. anti-Cuba policy -- seeks to isolate the government of Fidel Castro by stopping investment, particularly in property deemed by Washington to have been stolen from U.S. citizens.
Among other things it allows naturalised Americans to sue in U.S. courts foreign companies which have investments in property confiscated by Havana since the communist revolution of 1959.

This part has twice been suspended by U.S. President Bill Clinton -- the last time in January for six months -- but the EU and other countries have nevertheless protested at what they call the extra-territorial nature of the law.
The Washington Post reported on Friday that Clinton would attempt to convince Congress to modify the act if the EU suspended the WTO case.

The plan calls for the Europeans to "establish disciplines to deter" private companies in Europe from investing in property confiscated without compensation, not just in Cuba but globally, according to the report.
In exchange, Congress would be asked to relax some provisions of the act.

The Clinton administration has said the WTO does not have jurisdiction because the matter is not a trade dispute but a national security issue and has called on the Europeans to withdraw their complaint.

Trade experts are divided on predicting how any WTO case might go but most agree that if the United States was to cite national security interests, it would do so immediately after the EU presents its case on Monday.

They fear that if the U.S. government pursues this course, it will set a precedent that could seriously undermine the WTO, which took over the workings of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade in January 1995.
EU sources say Brittan is in frequent telephone contact with Stuart Eizenstat, the envoy appointed by Clinton to try to negotiate an end to the row.
Trade experts say it is difficult to see a way out of the impasse without either the EU or Washington losing face.

But they said any compromise was sure to be linked to the U.S. government also scrapping its "watchlist", which prohibits foreigners with links to companies proscribed by the State Department from visiting the United States.
They say, too, that the EU is certain to have to make more commitments to discouraging "legitimate" investment in Cuba and even scale back non-government aid to the Caribbean island
